record.title: Ordinary cost and mixer root updates

aligned_passages.text:
The full-support manuscript proves that an admissible integrable minimizer
of the zero-temperature Parisi functional for the pure zero-field
Sherrington–Kirkpatrick model has Stieltjes support equal to every overlap
scale in [0,1). The proof turns a hypothetical support gap into a constant
interval for the order parameter. Variational contact at the ends of that
interval conflicts with a strict curvature inequality inside it. Along the
auxiliary diffusion, the spatial gradient of the value function is a bounded
martingale. Full support makes this martingale's second moment equal to time;
its terminal correlation with Brownian motion gives the ground-state value.
The manuscript's further argument gives a smooth Stieltjes density, strictly
positive on $(0,1)$, and no atom at zero. Sections 9.1–9.2 derive this stronger
ordinary conclusion separately from the selected formal support statement.

This record reconstructs those arguments and follows the finite Gaussian
approximation into the separate QAOA manuscript. The latter claims that
finite deterministic circuits approach the SK optimum when system size tends
to infinity before circuit depth increases. Its circuit construction needs
additional approximation, synthesis, seed-removal and transfer arguments.
The two formal statements concern full support and scalar value
consequences; neither states QAOA circuit convergence. Their verification
scope is described at the end. See [OpenAI (2026a), §§1–2][fs-main] and
[OpenAI (2026b), Theorem 1.1][q-intro].

On a single spin, let $Z=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$ and
$X=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$; $Z_i$ and $X_i$ act on spin $i$
and as the identity on the other spins. Also set
$Y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}$ and
$|\pm\rangle=(|0\rangle\pm|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$.
Then $X|\pm\rangle=\pm|\pm\rangle$ and $Z|+\rangle=|-\rangle$. The cost and mixer are
$$
C_{n,J}=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}Z_iZ_j,\qquad B_n=\sum_iX_i.
$$
The two evolutions act differently:
$$
e^{-i\theta C_{n,J}}|\sigma\rangle
 =e^{-i\theta H_n(\sigma)}|\sigma\rangle,
\qquad
e^{-i\beta B_n}=\prod_{i=1}^n(\cos\beta\,I-i\sin\beta\,X_i).
$$
The cost evolution changes phases while preserving spin-basis probabilities;
the mixer combines amplitudes of different spin configurations. Cost evolution
alone leaves the initial uniform probabilities unchanged, and a mixer applied
first only multiplies $|+\rangle^{\otimes n}$ by $e^{-in\beta}$.
Alternating them lets the cost-dependent phases change subsequent measurement
probabilities. [Farhi, Goldstone, Gutmann and Zhou (2022), §2,
equations (1)–(6)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.08187v4).

A depth-$p$ state, with $p$ counting cost–mixer pairs, is
$$
|\psi_{n,p,J}(\boldsymbol\gamma,\boldsymbol\beta)\rangle
=e^{-i\beta_pB_n}e^{-i\gamma_pC_{n,J}}\cdots
 e^{-i\beta_1B_n}e^{-i\gamma_1C_{n,J}}|+\rangle^{\otimes n}.
$$
Here the real angle vectors $\boldsymbol\gamma,\boldsymbol\beta$ are
deterministic; $\boldsymbol\gamma$ is separate from the Parisi coefficient
$\gamma(t)$. A *word* means a finite ordered product of cost and mixer
exponentials. Its pattern and angles are fixed independently of $n,J$;
its cost operator depends on $n,J$. Define
$$
v_p(\boldsymbol\gamma,\boldsymbol\beta)
=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\mathbb E_J
 \langle\psi_{n,p,J}|C_{n,J}|\psi_{n,p,J}\rangle,
\qquad Q_p=\sup_{\boldsymbol\gamma,\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^p}v_p.
$$
The fixed-depth, fixed-angle infinite-size limit is the input from
Farhi, Goldstone, Gutmann and Zhou; it does not contain the later depth
conclusion; see [Farhi, Goldstone, Gutmann and Zhou (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.08187v4).
The source target is $\lim_{p\to\infty}Q_p=P_*$. Its needed lower
bound has the literal quantifiers
$$
\forall\varepsilon>0\quad\exists p\in\mathbb N,
\boldsymbol\gamma,\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^p:
\quad\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\mathbb E_J
\langle\psi_{n,p,J}|C_{n,J}|\psi_{n,p,J}\rangle
\ge P_*-\varepsilon.
$$
The same finite list of gates and angles is used for every $n,J$; this is
a limiting expected-energy conclusion. A cost expectation is bounded above by its
maximum eigenvalue, and zero-angle padding makes $Q_p$ nondecreasing.
It therefore suffices to construct one finite word for every accuracy.
Fixed-instance convergence at increasing depth is a different quantifier
order. Farhi, Goldstone and Gutmann's original QAOA argument obtains that
convergence by adiabatic evolution and its Trotter approximation, with depth
allowed to depend on the instance; it does not supply the size-independent
word required here. [Farhi–Goldstone–Gutmann (2014), equation (10) and
§VI, pp. 10–11](https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.4028v1);
[OpenAI (2026b), Theorem 1.1][q-intro].

The construction first describes local operations on a large tree, where
neighbouring subtrees supply Gaussian inputs. Temporary random labels let
those operations implement the finite classical function of §7. The hard
steps are to implement its aggregations using cost and mixer gates, and
then to replace every use of the labels by ordinary gates while preserving
the energy. Only the resulting ordinary word is transferred to SK.

The choices are nested: fix $\varepsilon$, choose $T<1$, choose a finite
mesh, fix the bounded classical formula and helper probabilities, then
choose the finite gate approximations and remove the seeds. The constants
in a replacement may depend on the surrounding word and on those positive
helper probabilities. [§8.6](#qaoa-assembly-detail) collects the error
allocation before the final $n\to\infty$ limit.
The principal circuit inputs can be read as four local lemmas. Their
proofs remain in the cited manuscript; §§8.2–8.5 reconstruct the
mechanisms and show where each hypothesis enters.

**Smooth replacement.** Fix the height, a finite expression and channel
list, and the required derivatives. Uniform recursive weighted bounds,
convergence of operators and adjoints, and strongly commuting signals with
the stated joint exponential bounds permit substitution inside a fixed
surrounding sequence in the exclusion-gate class defined in §8.2. Constants depend on that fixed family. This is the input
used in §8.3 to replace classical aggregates by finite gates; see
[the foundations, smooth topology and gate calculus][q-gate-calculus].

**Helper contraction and synthesis.** Fix a bounded, finite, type-excluded
odd formula, zero on helpers, and positive helper masses. The contraction
converges smoothly at every cut and for the specified responses. For each
$\eta>0$, finite seeded synthesis gives
$$
\mathcal E(v)\ge\mathcal E(m)-2\eta-2\sqrt{p_H}.
$$
Section 8.4 receives this one fixed seeded word. The source inputs are the
[synthesis statements][q-synthesis-statement] and
[helper theorem][q-helper-statement].

**Seed removal.** Fix that finite seeded word and an energy tolerance.
Reuse the same Gaussian at every occurrence on a vertex. Packet control and
the one-particle comparison then produce one finite ordinary word with the
required energy error. The [seed-removal theorem][q-seed-statement] supplies
an energy conclusion, not merely convergence of seed marginals. It makes the
ordinary-word transfer in §8.5 applicable.

**Fixed-word transfer.** Fix one ordinary word and all its angles before
either size or degree varies. Its positive tree scaled-edge limit equals
its SK expected-energy limit, with the convention conversion in §8.5.
This [fixed-word transfer][q-transfer] closes the thermodynamic-first
theorem in §8.6.

#### 8.1.1 One depth, three descriptions of the energy A single cost–mixer pair tests the signs and normalizations in this change of objects. Use the positive cost $C_{n,J}$ of §8 and $U=e^{-i\beta B_n}e^{-i\theta C_{n,J}}$; the symbol $\theta$ here is a cost angle, not the Parisi coefficient. Put $c=\cos(2\beta)$ and $s=\sin(2\beta)$. The Pauli identities are $$ e^{i\beta X}Ze^{-i\beta X}=cZ+sY,\qquad e^{i\alpha Z_iZ_j}Y_je^{-i\alpha Z_iZ_j} =Y_j\cos(2\alpha)+Z_iX_j\sin(2\alpha). $$ The mixed term $Z_iY_j$ therefore has cost-state expectation $$ \sin(2\theta J_{ij}/\sqrt n) \prod_{k\ne i,j}\cos(2\theta J_{jk}/\sqrt n). $$ The other mixed term exchanges $i$ and $j$. The $Z_iZ_j$ term has zero expectation. The $Y_iY_j$ term can be nonzero on an individual complete graph, but its expectation after the cost gate is independent of $J_{ij}$: $Y_iY_j$ commutes with that edge cost. Multiplying by $J_{ij}$ and averaging therefore removes it, even in the presence of triangles. For a standard Gaussian $J$, $$ \mathbb E\cos(aJ)=e^{-a^2/2},\qquad \mathbb E[J\sin(aJ)]=ae^{-a^2/2}. $$ Averaging the mixed terms and summing the $n(n-1)/2$ unordered edges gives $$ \frac1n\mathbb E_J\langle C_{n,J}\rangle =\frac{n-1}{n}\,\theta\sin(4\beta) e^{-2\theta^2(n-1)/n}. $$ This agrees with [Farhi et al., equation (62)][fggz]. With energy maximization, $\theta=1/2$, $\beta=\pi/8$ gives the limiting value $1/(2\sqrt e)$; their minimization example uses $\beta=-\pi/8$ and the negative value. For the positive cost $D^{-1/2}\sum_{\{i,j\}}Z_iZ_j$ on the $(D+1)$-regular tree, each endpoint has $D$ other neighbours. The same calculation now has no common-neighbour contribution and yields $$ \langle Z_oZ_v\rangle =\sin(4\beta)\sin(2\theta/\sqrt D) \cos^D(2\theta/\sqrt D). $$ Multiplying by $\sqrt D/2$ and letting $D\to\infty$ gives $\theta e^{-2\theta^2}\sin(4\beta)$, the same limit as finite SK. This checks the factor $1/2$ and the degree convention in §8.5. Finally let $e=Z\mathrm{vac}=|-\rangle\otimes\Omega$ and $Q=q(e)$ in the rooted description. Its vacuum law is standard normal. The depth-one root operation is $u=e^{-i\beta X}e^{-i\theta ZQ}$. Using $Y|+\rangle=-i|-\rangle$, its insertion is $$ v=u^*Zu\,\mathrm{vac} =|-\rangle\otimes[c-is\cos(2\theta Q)]\Omega +|+\rangle\otimes s\sin(2\theta Q)\Omega. $$ The root shift retains only the plus-root, one-particle component. The first-chaos coefficient of the sine is $\mathbb E[G\sin(2\theta G)]=2\theta e^{-2\theta^2}$, so $$ \mathsf L^*v=2\theta s e^{-2\theta^2}e,\qquad \operatorname{Re}\langle v,\mathsf Lv\rangle =2\theta sc e^{-2\theta^2} =\theta e^{-2\theta^2}\sin(4\beta). $$ Here $\operatorname{Re}\langle e,v\rangle=c$ supplies the final factor. Thus the observable, not just the Gaussian law, agrees in all three representations. The example uses the [ordinary root updates][q-ordinary-updates] and [root shift][q-root-energy]. It calibrates one depth; the higher-depth occupation and replacement hypotheses remain necessary.

### 8.2 Finite regularisation and the calculus needed for compilation Fix $T,N$ first. The independent continuous rounding coordinate makes the event at the sign discontinuity null. Bounded continuous odd approximations to that sign therefore converge in $L^2$ by dominated convergence. If the bounded output is $m^*$, shrink it to $(1-\kappa)m^*$, with fixed $0<\kappa<1$, before taking $\theta_\kappa=\tfrac12\arcsin((1-\kappa)m^*)$. This margin keeps the derivative of inverse sine bounded on its used range; the output loss is at most $\kappa$ in $L^2$. Then truncate the transmitted functions and approximate the resulting bounded maps by trigonometric polynomials. The source makes these choices from output toward leaves: each outer Lipschitz function is fixed before its inputs are approximated. The Gaussian isometry above converts an error in a transmitted child vector into the same $L^2$ error in its receiving position. Energy continuity then bounds the accumulated loss. The bounded output has the form $m=\sin(2\theta)$; it is the transmitted columns that are bounded, while the Gaussian fields themselves remain unbounded. [OpenAI (2026b), §3, bounded trigonometric approximation][q-bounded-classical]. **The formulas to be synthesized.** A mask is an event in the local seed space invariant under seed reversal. Fix a finite partition into masks, and write $p_R$ for the probability of mask $R$; probabilities used as denominators are positive. For disjoint masks $R,S$, aggregation on the finite regular tree means $$ (A_{RS}f)_i=\mathbf1_R(i)D^{-1/2} \sum_{j\sim i}\mathbf1_S(j)f_j. $$ A formula has a finite expression tree, with bounded measurable functions of the local seed as leaves. Internal operations are such aggregations or pointwise functions of previously formed quantities. Pointwise functions are smooth in their aggregate arguments, with polynomial bounds on all derivatives, uniformly in the seed. Seed dependence itself need not be smooth. Transmitted quantities are odd under simultaneous seed reversal; sent nonlinear functions and output angles are bounded, while aggregate Gaussian fields may be unbounded. An aggregation from $S$ to $R$ excludes $R$ if its transmitted formula uses no vertex of type $R$ below that call. All ancestor exclusions are retained, so a mask cannot recur on one active expression branch. It may recur on a different branch, and distinct branches may share descendants; exclusion asserts no independence between them. Gate targets are likewise excluded from the cross-edge dependencies of their parameters. This makes the physical all-neighbour calculation agree with the intended descendant calculation. For synthesis, reserve disjoint helper masks of positive mass, one per positive aggregation depth, absent from the output dependencies; the bounded odd output angle vanishes on their union. [OpenAI (2026b), Definition 3.3][q-formula-definition]; [Theorem 4.1][q-synthesis-statement]. The types can be encoded together with a Gaussian seed in one raw Gaussian variable: its sign supplies the odd symmetry, while disjoint binary digits of a uniform transform of its absolute value supply independent coordinates. The resulting finite type label is even and the Gaussian seed is odd under reversal. The associated pullback preserves vacuum, parity and $\mathsf L$. Thus adding types preserves the energy identification, rather than assuming an additional circuit resource. [OpenAI (2026b), §3, colours, exclusions and helpers][q-colors]. For the already fixed formula, the exclusion estimate is $$ \|m^{\rm col}-m\|^2\le C(\alpha+p_H), $$ where $\alpha$ is the largest nonhelper type mass and $p_H$ is the total helper mass. Its constant is independent of the number of types. The proof uses orthogonality of the disjoint masks before applying the Lipschitz estimate in the original, fixed list of formula coordinates. Treating the refined types as an arbitrary growing list of independent arguments would not provide this bound. The resulting classical near-optimality proposition supplies a finite bounded odd formula, zero on helpers, with energy as close to $P_*$ as required. [OpenAI (2026b), §3, “Type exclusion at small cost” and “Classical near-optimality in synthesis form”][q-colors]. **Which convergence permits the later substitutions?** The gate calculus uses recursive weights $\mathsf W_{h+1}=\mathsf W_0+d\Gamma(\Lambda_h)$, where $\Lambda_h$ is the previous weight restricted to the centred child space. The local weight includes the unbounded raw seed when needed. Its smooth domain is the intersection of all weighted domains. Smooth bounds mean polynomial bounds, with a finite loss of weight powers, for the maps, their adjoints and every specified parameter derivative. The finite height, fixed expression and fixed number of channels matter in these estimates. Strong convergence together with uniform stronger weighted bounds gives convergence in each weaker weighted norm by a spectral cutoff. This is the topology in which one replaces a gate inside a fixed surrounding circuit. [OpenAI (2026b), §2, weights and the topology of convergence][q-weights]. More precisely, the imported smooth-convergence contract is: for each output power $m$ and parameter multi-index $\alpha$, there are an input power $r$, exponent $k$ and constant $C$ such that $$ \|\mathsf W_D^m\partial_x^\alpha F_D(x)\xi\| \le C(1+|x|)^k\|\mathsf W_D^r\xi\|, \qquad \xi\in\bigcap_{q\ge0}\operatorname{Dom}(\mathsf W_D^q). $$ The bound is uniform in degree $D$ and parameter $x$. The same bound and strong convergence on smooth inputs are required for the adjoints and all specified parameter derivatives, with compatible limiting adjoints. Constants may depend on the fixed expression, height, channel list and derivative order. Bounded adjoint derivatives alone do not supply their convergence. At bounded local seeds $\mathsf W_0=1$; for polynomial Gaussian growth the source uses the vacuum-preserving weight $P_0+Q_0(1+|s|)Q_0$, where $P_0$ projects to the local vacuum and $Q_0=1-P_0$. These recursive weights control every generation. They differ from the top-generation number weight in §8.4's packet argument. No uniformity in growing word length, vanishing helper mass or the later seed-removal parameter is implicit in this contract. [OpenAI (2026b), §2, smooth-family bound][q-weights]. One of the essential inputs retains a term beyond the Gaussian field. Let $K_D(x)$ be a smooth unitary family with $K_D(0)=1$, uniformly controlled derivatives and adjoint derivatives that converge smoothly in the stated weighted topology to those of a limiting family $K$, and centred first vacuum derivatives. Write $K_\alpha=\partial_\alpha K(0)=iT_\alpha$ and $K_{\alpha\lambda}=\partial_\alpha\partial_\lambda K(0)$. For a fixed finite parameter list $a$, the source proves $$ K_D(a/\sqrt D)^{\otimes D}\longrightarrow \exp\!\left\{ i\sum_\alpha a_\alpha q(T_\alpha\mathrm{vac}) +\frac12\sum_{\alpha,\lambda}a_\alpha a_\lambda \left\langle K_{\alpha\lambda} +\tfrac12\{T_\alpha,T_\lambda\}\right\rangle_0 \right\}. $$ The second term is imaginary by unitarity. It survives because a second-order change of size $D^{-1}$ occurs in each of $D$ children. Its scalar coefficients become a possibly nonconstant controlled operator when commuting signals replace $a$. For example, $K(x)=e^{ix^2}$ has zero first derivative at zero but $K(a/\sqrt D)^D=e^{ia^2}$ exactly. Keeping only the first derivative would miss even this elementary contribution. The example explains why the term is necessary; the source's weighted product lemma supplies the general convergence and domain bounds. [OpenAI (2026b), §2, “Products of small unitaries”][q-unitary]. Commuting substitution is justified through a joint spectral calculus and Fourier estimates. It requires the physical control algebra, the self-adjoint signal operators and receiving seed to strongly commute, with joint exponential and weighted derivative bounds as stated in the source. This is stronger than a formal commutator identity on one domain. It does not require a nonsingular covariance matrix or an inverse Gram matrix. Exclusions establish that commuting algebra before a preceding circuit is conjugated through it; conjugation preserves commutation even when the signals share descendants. [OpenAI (2026b), §2, “Smooth commuting substitution”][q-substitution]. The exact cut recursion records the effect of such shared lower calculations. Let $y$ be the incoming boundary data, $V(y)$ the root matrix, and $m(y)$ its outgoing signals in the current frame. Factoring out the operations wholly inside each child gives $$ E^{[d]}(y)=V(y)\prod_{j\ \mathrm{child}} K_j^{[d-1]}(D^{-1/2}m(y)),\qquad K^{[d]}(y)=u^*E^{[d]}(0)^*E^{[d]}(y)u. $$ Every ratio $K^{[d]}$ equals one at zero. Nevertheless $m(0)$ generally does not vanish, because removing the parent input leaves the root's own signals. The actual zero-boundary root update is $u_{\rm new}=E^{[d]}(0)u$. It is not recovered by setting the entire ratio to one and discarding the baseline operation. Applying the unitary product lemma to this recursion, and then commuting substitution, is the source's smooth gate calculus. Its replacement statement covers a fixed finite surrounding sequence and its required parameter derivatives; it does not assert uniformity for arbitrary sequences whose length or channel count grows. [OpenAI (2026b), §2, smooth gate calculus and its cut recursion][q-gate-calculus].

### 8.4 Removing the seed controls without changing their joint law Seed removal must simulate one Gaussian variable per vertex, reused at all seed gates. Replacing each occurrence with a fresh independent Gaussian would change the circuit. The source proves a theorem for any already fixed finite seeded word and any energy tolerance, producing one finite ordinary word. Its proof works in the fixed-word tree limit; it does not take a degree limit simultaneously with its small parameter. [OpenAI (2026b), §5, “Removal of seed controls”][q-seed-statement]. **A small component supplies a large response.** Fix $b>0$ and $01$. The right side is $o(r)$: within each ordinary packet the relevant Hermitian expectation is real, distinct packet centres have overlap $O(r^M)$, and terms containing only special packets have size $O(r^2)$. The norm remainder is carried by unitarity; it receives no unproved occupation bound. The exact zero clocks then cancel the first-order displacement on ordinary packets, leaving $o(r)$ error there. The prescribed action on a normalized special packet has $o(1)$ error, multiplied by its $O(r)$ amplitude. These are the unequal accuracy requirements that the next echo uses. [OpenAI (2026b), §5, accuracy of selective probes][q-seed-selective]. **The echo amplifies a controlled difference.** Consider a forward cost $t/r$, a selective flip of the special component, the reverse cost $-t/r$, and a selective undoing of that flip. The packet invariant transports the special component so that its contribution to the insertion changes sign. For the actual insertion directions before and after the first flip, it gives $$ v'_r-v_r=-2r\,w_r+o(r). $$ The Weyl product of the two costs is formed with these actual directions before making any approximation. Their large centres cancel, leaving a bounded displacement $$ \frac tr(v'_r-v_r)=-2t\,w_r+o(1). $$ Approximating each direction by a low component with merely $O(r)$ error before this subtraction would leave an uncontrolled order-one error. The remaining scalar Weyl phase is independent of the root spin and cancels in insertions; it need not itself converge. The second flip restores the transported special component so that the same construction can be used again. Mixers receive analogous selective compensations. [OpenAI (2026b), §5, packet invariant, insertion approximation and “One echo”][q-seed-echo]. In the limit, $\ell_r$ and $w_r$ become two orthogonal external real Gaussian modes at each root. The initialization uses $q(\ell)$ and every simulated seed gate uses the same $q(w)$: choosing $t=\sigma/2$ implements $e^{-i\sigma Zq(w)}$. Different vertices have independent local copies. This is the required joint law of the seeded word. A finite induction uses the Weyl identity $$ \langle W(f)\Omega,W(g)\Omega\rangle =\exp\!\left(-\tfrac12\|g-f\|^2 +i\operatorname{Im}\langle f,g\rangle\right) $$ to match the relevant finite Gram matrices. Escaping high directions supply precisely the vanishing pairings between the new external modes and endogenous child directions. [OpenAI (2026b), §5, external-mode limit][q-seed-gram]. **The energy pairing after seed removal.** Matching the seed law and its finite Gram matrices is not yet enough. For a centred low insertion $h=\sum_j s_j\otimes W(f_j)\Omega$, the one-particle coefficient of $W(f_j)\Omega$ is $i e^{-\|f_j\|^2/2}f_j$. Hence $$ \langle h,\mathsf Lh\rangle =-i\sum_j\langle s_j,+\rangle e^{-\|f_j\|^2/2} \langle f_j,h\rangle. $$ In the seeded representation, $\mathsf L$ places the root-seed factor in its vacuum and creates $h$ only in the endogenous child space. External components therefore contribute zero to the last pairing. The high-direction estimate yields the same zeros in the actual limit. The actual insertion differs from its low insertion by $O(r)$, so energy continuity completes the comparison. Matching Gram matrices without this one-particle calculation would not identify $\mathsf L$ or its energy. [OpenAI (2026b), §5, “Finite Gram induction,” including the energy calculation][q-seed-gram]. **Why the selective rotations are available at every required stage.** The limiting projection of each special centre must be nonzero. The source imposes finitely many visibility conditions on the angles of the formal seeded word. At each relevant standard stage they have form $$ -2\operatorname{Im}\langle v_Z^{\rm form}, -2bz\,e+yD^{\rm form}\rangle\ne0, \qquad z,y\in\{\pm1\}, $$ where $e=Z\mathrm{vac}$ and $D^{\rm form}$ accumulates echoes whose reverse costs have already occurred. These functions are real analytic by the finite Weyl formulas. Setting all target angles to zero, while retaining initialization, gives $4bz e^{-8b^2}\ne0$, so none is identically zero. An arbitrarily small angle perturbation avoids their finite union of zero sets and the zero echo-time hyperplanes. The huge-cost stages need a separate transverse-projection estimate; their limiting projection pairs then also have a nonzero coordinate. Finite pulse lists can now be chosen successively from limits already established at earlier stages. No list is chosen from a limit that assumes its own successful implementation. [OpenAI (2026b), §5, huge-stage transverse projection, visibility and construction order][q-seed-visibility]. The choices are therefore nested: make $b$ small to control initialization; perturb the fixed target angles to ensure visibility; choose all finite probe lists; finally choose $r$ small. A value of $r$ fixes every large angle and every finite product. The theorem allows those angles to be large or negative. It makes no claim of uniform bounds as the target word length grows or as the tolerance tends to zero. [OpenAI (2026b), §5, proof of seed removal][q-seed-visibility].

### 8.5 Transfer of the resulting ordinary word After all these choices there is one finite ordinary word $W$, fixed independently of degree, size and disorder. On the $(D+1)$-regular tree use $C_D=D^{-1/2}\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}Z_iZ_j$, counting each edge once. The edge expectation is defined on the finite light cone described in §8.1. The source applies the fixed-word transfer theorem $$ v_W=\lim_{D\to\infty}\frac{\sqrt D}{2} \langle+|W_D^*Z_iZ_jW_D|+\rangle. $$ The [full preprint of Basso et al., arXiv:2110.14206v3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.14206v3), Theorem 1, equates the limiting tree recursion with the infinite-size SK recursion for every fixed depth and fixed angle vector. Its proof is in §6, especially (6.6)–(6.31), with the symmetry statement proved in Appendix B and the iteration stabilisation in Appendix A.4. The shorter proceedings edition states the theorem but refers to this full preprint for the proof. Basso et al. use a negative tree cost in (2.3). Let $V=\prod_{i\in A}X_i$ on one bipartition of the finite light cone. Every edge has exactly one endpoint in $A$, hence $$ VZ_iZ_jV=-Z_iZ_j,\qquad VB_DV=B_D,\qquad V|+\rangle=|+\rangle. $$ Consequently, if $C_D^-=-C_D$, then $VW(C_D^-,B_D)V=W(C_D,B_D)$ for the same fixed word and angles, while its measured edge expectation changes sign. This converts the negative cut convention in their (2.6) to the positive energy above. Their SK cost (6.1) already has the positive convention used here. The result applies after seed removal; it does not directly transfer an arbitrary seeded or controlled word. It also supplies no joint limit in which depth or angles change with $D$ or $n$. [OpenAI (2026b), §2, “Fixed-word transfer”][q-transfer]. For an ordinary cost or mixer the root updates are, respectively, $$ u\longmapsto e^{-itZq(v_Z)}u, \qquad u\longmapsto e^{-i\beta X}u, \qquad v_Z=u^*Zu\,\mathrm{vac}. $$ The source proves smooth convergence for these updates, their adjoints and fixed angle derivatives. The resulting occupation bounds supply the hypothesis of the root-shift energy proposition in §8.1. Thus its energy is the scaled edge limit required for transfer. Finally merge consecutive gates of the same type and insert zero-angle gates where needed to express $W$ in alternating QAOA form. [OpenAI (2026b), §2, “Ordinary root updates”][q-ordinary-updates].

### 8.6 Fixing the word before the thermodynamic limit Allocate errors after choosing the desired $\varepsilon>0$. Apply the classical near-optimality proposition with the two tolerances $\varepsilon/4$ and $\eta_H=(\varepsilon/8)^2$. It supplies one formula and its helper law together, with classical loss below $\varepsilon/4$ and $0P_*-3\varepsilon/4. $$ Seed removal uses less than $\varepsilon/4$. The resulting fixed ordinary word therefore satisfies $v_W>P_*-\varepsilon$ after the fixed-word transfer. Its thermodynamic limit is taken only after all approximation choices have been made. Since $Q_p\le P_*$ and zero padding makes $Q_p$ nondecreasing, this proves the source's thermodynamic-first conclusion from its stated analytic inputs. [OpenAI (2026b), §6][q-assembly]. The order is: accuracy; minimizer and fixed $T<1$; finite scalar mesh; smoothing and bounded approximations; finite types and positive helper masses; exact helper contractions and finite commutator products; one fixed seeded word; initialization size; generic angle perturbation; finite selective pulse lists; sufficiently small $r$; one ordinary word; its $n\to\infty$ limit. The degree limits identify the rooted calculus and the transferred value for each already fixed word; they do not license changing that word with the finite instance. The reconstruction makes the source's circuit mechanisms explicit, but the evidence classes remain separate. The scalar construction and its formal interfaces in §§6–7 and 12 do not by themselves establish the weighted unitary calculus, simultaneous helper contraction or seed removal. Those analytic theorems are additional inputs from the QAOA manuscript, with the domain, commutation and uniformity hypotheses specified above. No quantitative depth bound, finite-size rate, efficient angle-selection procedure, or independent formal verification of this entire circuit construction follows from the selected formal statements. This completes the main support-to-circuit proof. The later comparisons have separate purposes: [§11.1](#positive-temperature-route) gives another classical input; [§11.2](#fixed-word-probability) adds a second-moment sampling theorem; and [§§11.3–11.5](#depth-quantifiers) compare quantifiers, other models and later finite-size estimates. They are not further premises of the proof just completed.

After clipping and bounded approximation, the result enters the same synthesis and seed-removal route as the primary construction. Its source dependencies and fixed-temperature choice of parameters remain separate from the retained zero-temperature formal interfaces. For each $\eta>0$ it selects one finite depth and normalized angles, and then a degree threshold, such that every finite simple unweighted $(D+1)$-regular graph of girth greater than $2p+1$ has expected cut fraction at least $$ \frac12+\frac{P_*-\eta}{\sqrt D} $$ for all sufficiently large $D$. The usual MaxCut cost is $H_{\rm MC}=\frac12\sum_{\{i,j\}}(I-Z_iZ_j)$, so its angles are $2\boldsymbol\gamma/\sqrt D$: the normalized angles are fixed, while these physical cost angles depend on degree. The sign conversion uses a bipartition of the relevant tree neighbourhood of each edge; the whole graph need not be bipartite. The further optimality comparison is for a uniform simple labelled $(D+1)$-regular graph $G_{n,D+1}$, along sizes with $n(D+1)$ even. Write $\operatorname{OPT}(G)$ for the maximum cut size divided by $|E(G)|$, $q_{p,G}$ for the circuit's expected cut fraction, and $\Delta_D(G)=\operatorname{OPT}(G)-q_{p,G}(2\boldsymbol\gamma/\sqrt D, \boldsymbol\beta)$. The same word can be chosen so that $$ \lim_{D\to\infty} \limsup_{\substack{n\to\infty\\n(D+1)\ \mathrm{even}}} \Pr_G\{\sqrt D\,\Delta_D(G_{n,D+1})>\eta\}=0. $$ Size goes to infinity first at fixed degree and word. The probability is over the random graph; the cut fraction has already averaged the quantum measurement. For fixed $D,p$, [McKay, Wormald and Wysocka (2004), Theorem 1](https://doi.org/10.37236/1819), gives tight counts of cycles of lengths at most $2p+3$. Every edge with a nontree neighbourhood is within bounded distance of one of these cycles, so their fraction tends to zero. The optimum is supplied separately by [Dembo, Montanari and Sen, arXiv:1503.03923v2, Theorem 1.6(b)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.03923v2): dividing their cut size per vertex by $(D+1)/2$ gives the leading cut fraction $1/2+P_*/\sqrt{D+1}$, with an error $o(D^{-1/2})$ in the stated iterated regime. A high-girth lower bound alone would not prove optimality on every high-girth graph. See [OpenAI (2026b), Corollary 1.2 and its complete proof][q-maxcut]. This separate consequence is recorded to preserve the source's scope; it is not a new selected formal endpoint or a joint size–degree limit.
